title: Why ExxonMobil and Chevron Reminded Investors to Keep it Simple - MarketBeat
content:
Some of 2026's best large-cap stories didn't come from Silicon Valley. They came from Texas. At the market close on Nov. 3, Chevron Corp. NYSE: CVX was up more than 46% over the past year. ExxonMobil NYSE: XOM has had an even more impressive run, up nearly 56%. Both stocks also pay dividends that keep growing. Chevron yields about 3% and has raised its payout for 38 straight years. ExxonMobil's streak of annual dividend increases now stands at 42 years with a yield of around 2.3%. Yet many investors spent the year looking elsewhere. Capital chased artificial intelligence (AI) and the technology names tied to it. Energy stocks were treated as a trade on oil prices rather than on the businesses themselves. The trade seemed simple: when crude cools off, so will these stocks. Third-quarter results, released by Chevron and ExxonMobil on Oct. 30, challenge that view. Higher prices helped. But refining strength, cost discipline and balance sheet repair did much of the work. Both companies also absorbed accounting headwinds that should reverse. That sets up a case for further upside, even after a big year. Chevron reported adjusted earnings of $10.4 billion, or $5.28 per share. That's up from $1.85 per share a year ago. Brent crude averaged $97 per barrel versus $69, lifting upstream results. But the bigger swing came from refining. Downstream earnings jumped to $4.9 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier. Chevron's U.S. refineries processed a record 1.09 million barrels per day. Crude unit utilization reached nearly 98%. That matters because refining profits depend on margins, not just crude prices. Strong margins offset a 109,000 barrel-per-day drop in international production. Chevron tied that decline to price-driven entitlement effects and the Middle East conflict. Cash flow tells the rest of the story. Chevron generated $16 billion in operating cash flow and $12 billion in free cash flow. It paid $3.5 billion in dividends and repurchased $2.5 billion of stock. It still cut total debt by $3.5 billion. Net debt fell $7.8 billion in the quarter alone. Management also laid out a growth path. Chevron's Venezuelan joint ventures plan to invest $7 billion over five years. The company says that could more than double production there. In the Bakken, new agreements should cut midstream costs by roughly 50%. Both moves aim to improve returns per barrel, not just add volume. ExxonMobil posted adjusted earnings of $17.5 billion, or $4.23 per share. That compares with $3.52 per share in the second quarter. GAAP earnings came in at $3.72 per share. Operating cash flow totaled $25.7 billion, and free cash flow reached $19.1 billion. Like Chevron, ExxonMobil leaned on refining. Adjusted Energy Products earnings more than doubled from the prior quarter to $9.1 billion. Its U.S. Gulf Coast refineries ran at 100% crude unit utilization. Meanwhile, upstream earnings fell on lower prices and a Guyana entitlement impact. The integrated model did exactly what it was built to do. CEO Darren Woods made a point investors should note. He described the gains as lasting improvements, not just the product of favorable pricing. ExxonMobil estimates its structural cost savings at $16.9 billion since 2019. Lower costs reduce the oil price needed to keep earnings and dividends growing. Shareholders are getting paid along the way. ExxonMobil returned $9.4 billion in the quarter, including $5.1 billion in buybacks. It plans $20 billion in repurchases for 2027. It also declared a $1.07 quarterly dividend. Net debt has fallen by nearly $11 billion so far this year. Both reports carried a detail that's easy to miss. Rising oil prices created "timing effects" that reduced reported earnings. These come mainly from marking derivatives to market before physical barrels are delivered. Chevron absorbed $1.58 billion in negative timing effects. ExxonMobil's hit totaled roughly $2.5 billion. ExxonMobil notes these impacts are expected to unwind in later periods. In other words, part of the third quarter's profit was deferred, not lost. If prices stabilize, that reversal could boost results in the coming quarters. It's a potential catalyst many investors may not be watching. None of this makes these stocks completely safe. Future results still depend heavily on commodity prices and refining margins. Both are elevated partly because of the Middle East conflict. If supply disruptions ease, margins could compress quickly. Chevron's total production also slipped from a year ago, which bears watching. Valuation is less forgiving after a 50% run. Investors buying now are paying for continued strength. That makes execution over the next few quarters more important, not less. The lesson from this quarter isn't complicated. Two of the world's largest energy companies are generating enormous amounts of cash. They're cutting debt, buying back stock, and raising dividends. And they're doing it with growing help from refining and cost cuts, not just oil prices. Investors who chased complexity this year may have overlooked that simplicity. For those still on the sidelines, the latest results suggest the story isn't finished. Patient, income-focused investors may find that keeping it simple still pays. title: Exxon Mobil Drops 4.2% in a Single Session to $167.68 - 24/7 Wall St.
content: As seen on the 24/7 Wall St. homepage on November 4, 2026. A 4.20% slide to $167.68 wipes roughly $28.7 billion off a $684 billion megacap, a rare single-session move for one of the market's steadiest large caps. Moves this size here usually reset the whole energy complex's tone. Exxon Mobil slid roughly 4.2% to close near $167.68, erasing about $28.7 billion in market value. That is a striking single-day loss for a stock long regarded as one of the most stable names in large-cap equities. Exxon Mobil rarely posts intraday swings of this magnitude, so when it does, traders across the energy sector take notice. Moves of this size in a name this large tend to reset the tone for the broader energy complex. The decline came as a steady grind lower that accelerated through the afternoon. That kind of sustained, directional selling over several hours is typically a signal of broad-based institutional pressure rather than a brief algorithmic spike. For investors already holding the stock, the session illustrates how quickly a megacap energy position can shed value even without an obvious single catalyst visible in the data. For those watching from the sidelines, the day's slide creates real urgency around understanding what drove the move before the next session begins. 51 stocks printed fresh 52-week highs this week, and the leadership is energy plus big biotech: Cheniere cleared its prior peak by 11.7%, with Regeneron, Eli Lilly and Gilead all stretching more than 8% past theirs. The biggest US refiner saying diesel is where the system is tightest points to fatter distillate margins for anyone with refining capacity, and higher fuel costs for everyone else. Exxon is adding diesel barrels into the tightest diesel market in years, with the IEA warning the global crunch drags into 2027. The Beaumont expansion is why its Gulf Coast distillate volumes keep climbing while rivals shutter capacity. Woods is making the case that Exxon's earnings power now survives a weaker oil tape, with EIA forecasting lower crude prices into 2026 and 2027. For holders of a $753.7 billion major, the cost base is the variable management actually controls. Exxon Mobil's second 52-week high in a week, $183.21, clears the October 16 mark by 2.36% and extends a run that has added roughly $70 a share since late October 2025. A $753.3 billion megacap moving like this is doing real work for index holders. A $4.5 billion refining tailwind flagged ahead of Q3 results resets the bar for Exxon and the whole energy complex. 54 stocks printed fresh 52-week highs this week, and Big Oil showed up in force: Suncor, BP, Shell, Phillips 66, Petrobras and Exxon all cleared prior peaks. Moderna led the whole list, topping its old high by 16%. Cramer is pulling money toward consumer staples, retailers and oils while the data center complex cracks, and he is framing Schwab's selloff on AI-agent worries as a repeat of the 2023 banking scare that proved a buying opportunity. For anyone concentrated in AI hardware, the Oracle half-sell is the clearest sell discipline he offered all episode. Exxon Mobil cleared its March 30 peak with a 52-week high at $172.15. The major has spent six months stuck below that line and just broke through. Arm closed up 17.19% at $323, topping a session where four other priority names each added more than 12%. Declines stayed shallow: Novo Nordisk's 7.94% drop was the only one past 4%, with Exxon Mobil and Chevron down under 3%. For readers following US Oil and Gas Stocks, the results showed how the company's integrated model can perform in a volatile energy market. Geopolitical tension, including conflicts affecting energy supply, has pushed fuel prices higher this year. That backdrop supported refining profits, while the company's own cost discipline and project execution helped lift cash generation. The standout performer was the energy products segment, which includes refining. Earnings in this business more than doubled from the previous quarter, driven by higher margins and strong operations. Global refining utilisation reached a record, with US Gulf Coast crude units running close to full capacity. Refining profits tend to rise when fuel demand is strong and supply is tight. With gasoline and diesel prices elevated, ExxonMobil's large refining network was well positioned to benefit. Chemical product earnings declined as margins weakened, reflecting softer industrial demand and new global capacity. Specialty products, which include lubricants and base stocks, improved on better margins. Together, these segments show the diversity of the company's earnings base. Upstream earnings fell from the previous quarter, reflecting lower crude prices during the period and production entitlement effects in Guyana. Overall output stayed broadly stable. Even so, the long-term growth story in upstream remains strong. Guyana's Stabroek block surpassed a major cumulative production milestone just over a decade after discovery, described as the fastest ramp of any major offshore development. The Permian Basin in Texas and New Mexico also continued to deliver strong volumes. Management pointed to large structural cost savings achieved over recent years, which have strengthened earnings across commodity cycles. Automation is expanding in the Permian, with automated drilling rigs expected to cover a growing share of the fleet in coming years. The company also highlighted technology transfer between businesses. Refining expertise helped develop a lighter material used in drilling, an example of how integration can create advantages that standalone producers may lack. ExxonMobil is taking over operatorship of the Papua LNG project and increasing its stake, reinforcing its position in liquefied natural gas. LNG demand is expected to grow as countries look for cleaner alternatives to coal and secure energy supplies. In carbon capture, the company started another operation for an outside customer and gained approval for a new storage project. These businesses remain small but offer long-term options as industrial customers seek to reduce emissions. Strong cash flow supported continued dividends and share repurchases. The company is in its fifth decade of consecutive annual dividend increases and confirmed plans to keep repurchases at a similar pace next year. Net debt also declined during the quarter, strengthening an already solid balance sheet. This combination of rising dividends and repurchases is a key reason many income-focused investors follow the stock, particularly in a market where few large companies offer such a long payout record. ExxonMobil's strategy rests on investing in advantaged assets that remain profitable even when oil prices fall. Guyana and the Permian are central to that approach because they combine large resources with relatively low production costs. LNG projects add long-term contracted cash flows that are less sensitive to short-term price swings. Management has also emphasised capital discipline. Rather than spending heavily when prices are high, the company aims to keep investment steady and return excess cash to investors. That consistency has supported confidence in the dividend through several energy cycles. Refining and chemicals give the company a natural hedge. When crude prices fall, refining margins may improve because input costs drop, partly cushioning the impact on upstream earnings. This balance is a key reason large integrated companies are viewed as more resilient than pure producers. Energy prices remain volatile and tied to geopolitics, supply decisions by major producers and economic growth. Refining margins can fall quickly if demand weakens or new capacity arrives. Regulatory and climate policies also shape long-term investment decisions. As a heavyweight member of the NYSE Composite, ExxonMobil remains a bellwether for the US energy sector. The coming quarters will test whether refining strength persists and whether upstream growth in Guyana and the Permian continues on schedule. For now, the quarter highlights a company using its scale, integration and cost control to deliver solid results even as individual segments move in different directions. Low-cost production remains a focus across the portfolio. By concentrating capital on the most profitable barrels and steadily lowering break-even levels, ExxonMobil aims to keep generating cash even if prices fall sharply from current levels, a priority that management has repeated throughout the year. title: Will ExxonMobil's 100,000-BPD Diesel Expansion Boost Refining Profit? - TradingView
content: ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM is focusing on expanding its refining operations to increase the production of higher-value fuels, particularly diesel, and strengthen long-term profitability. The company expects its investments across U.S. refineries to increase distillate production by another 100,000 barrels per day (BPD). This expansion is part of XOM's broader strategy to improve its product mix and enhance earnings and cash flow. According to media reports citing ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods' Oct. 30, 2026, CNBC interview, the company plans to allocate approximately 10% of its more than $100 billion capital investment program for 2027-2030 toward refining operations, representing roughly $10 billion in planned spending. The integrated energy giant has already invested around $17 billion in refining since 2019, increasing crude processing capacity by nearly 10% over the period. Projects such as the Beaumont refinery expansion have contributed to a roughly 40% increase in U.S. Gulf Coast distillate production, while ongoing work at Baytown is aimed at expanding output. Beyond capacity additions, XOM has reduced refinery turnaround costs by about 30%, reflecting improved operational efficiency. The expansion comes as global refining capacity constraints have tightened fuel supplies and supported stronger refining margins. XOM's expanded trading and optimization capabilities allow it to secure advantaged feedstocks and direct refined products to higher-value markets. The planned increase in diesel production, combined with ongoing investments and improved operating efficiency, is expected to enhance ExxonMobil's earnings and cash flow, although profitability remains dependent on refining market conditions. The focus on increasing higher-value fuel production extends beyond ExxonMobil, with Valero Energy Corporation VLO and Marathon Petroleum Corporation MPC investing in refining efficiency and product optimization. During its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, Valero Energy highlighted improvements in its product mix following the completion of the $230 million St. Charles refinery optimization project. Meanwhile, Marathon Petroleum emphasized that investments at its Garyville and Robinson facilities have enhanced operating flexibility and supported higher distillate yields. While VLO is working to strengthen its refining competitiveness through operational improvements, MPC remains focused on optimizing its refining network to support profitability. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation XOM emphasized refining competitiveness, global LNG expansion and disciplined capital allocation during its third-quarter 2026 earnings call. Management highlighted how long-term investments and operational improvements are strengthening the company's ability to navigate volatile energy markets. The discussion also addressed Middle East supply disruptions, production growth opportunities and the sustainability of shareholder distributions across commodity cycles. The company reported adjusted EPS of $4.23, exceeding the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $3.90. Revenues of $113.16 billion surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $102.98 billion by 9.90%. ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | ExxonMobil Holdings Corporation Quote Chairman and CEO Darren Woods emphasized that refinery modernization remains central to ExxonMobil's strategy. The company is prioritizing higher-value products rather than pursuing large-scale capacity additions. During a Morgan Stanley analyst's questions, Woods explained that upgrading existing facilities can cost roughly half as much as constructing new plants. Projects at Baytown, Baton Rouge and Beaumont are designed to increase diesel, lubricant and chemical feedstock output. Senior Vice President and CFO Neil Hansen noted that diesel yields have improved approximately 3.5% since 2019. This improvement generated $3.5 billion in additional year-to-date margins, demonstrating the financial contribution of refinery investments. Capital allocation received considerable attention following ExxonMobil's announcement of a 4% dividend increase, extending its streak of annual dividend growth to 44 consecutive years. Responding to a Goldman Sachs analyst, Woods reiterated management's preference for predictable shareholder distributions rather than adjusting payouts aggressively with commodity prices. ExxonMobil plans to maintain annual share repurchases of $20 billion in 2027, assuming reasonable market conditions. Hansen emphasized balance-sheet flexibility as essential to sustaining this approach. The company distributed $9.4 billion during the quarter, comprising $4.3 billion in dividends and $5.1 billion in repurchases. ExxonMobil is expanding its international natural gas portfolio while seeking greater operational control over major developments. Woods highlighted agreements to increase ownership in Papua LNG to 34% and Rovuma LNG in Mozambique to 50%. Management believes operatorship allows ExxonMobil to apply its technical and project execution capabilities more effectively. During the analyst discussion, Woods reaffirmed expectations for a Rovuma final investment decision before year-end 2026. At Golden Pass LNG, Train 2 is expected to reach substantial completion by December, while Train 3 mechanical completion is targeted for mid-2027. Upstream development remains focused on improving resource recovery and operating efficiency rather than pursuing production volumes alone. Woods told an Evercore analyst that Permian production had reached its year-end target ahead of schedule. ExxonMobil currently operates three automated drilling rigs and expects these systems to represent approximately half its Permian fleet by 2028. In Guyana, cumulative Stabroek Block production surpassed 1 billion barrels. Management expects the Uaru development to begin production in the fourth quarter, supporting continued growth from the offshore portfolio. Geopolitical disruption remained a significant discussion topic, particularly regarding global refined-product shortages and LNG transportation constraints. Woods told a UBS analyst that restoring normal product supply depends partly on reopening Middle East export routes, repairing damaged refining facilities and increasing available capacity elsewhere. He indicated normalization could extend well through 2027. During questions from Piper Sandler, Woods clarified that Qatar accounted for much of the production disruption. UAE production had largely recovered, although logistical restrictions continued delaying sales realization. Management consistently emphasized operational control, technological improvements and disciplined investment as foundations for future earnings growth. Woods maintained that ExxonMobil intends to pursue opportunities beyond 2030 while avoiding premature commitments. President and Treasurer James Chapman also confirmed that updated 2027 planning metrics would be communicated through a press release later in 2026. title: Why Did MO, GILD, XOM Stocks Surge To 52-Week Highs Last Week? - TradingView
content: Altria Group (MO), Gilead Sciences (GILD) and ExxonMobil (XOM) stocks ascended to fresh 52-week highs on Friday after strong third-quarter results, improved earnings outlooks and higher shareholder returns boosted investor confidence. Strong tobacco pricing, growing HIV drug sales and improved refining margins supported gains across the three companies. Altria and ExxonMobil stocks gained 1% and 2%, respectively, while Gilead Sciences stock climbed 3%. Altria Gains After Earnings Beat And Higher Outlook Altria stock reached a record high of $79.81 after the tobacco company delivered better-than-expected third-quarter (Q3) 2026 results. Adjusted earnings came in at $1.52 per share, narrowly exceeding Wall Street's $1.51 estimate, as per Fiscal.ai. Revenue, excluding excise taxes, increased 3.6% from a year earlier to $5.44 billion. The company raised its 2026 earnings forecast to $5.66 - $5.74 per share and increased its stock buyback plan by another $1 billion. UBS raised its price target on MO to $83 from $79 and kept a ‘Buy’ rating. Morgan Stanley lifted its price target to $77 from $71 but maintained an ‘Equal Weight’ rating, citing weakness in traditional cigarette sales. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘neutral’ territory. Gilead Sciences stock touched an all-time high of $175.65 after exceeding Q3 revenue and earnings expectations. Its HIV business remained a major growth engine, supported by demand for treatments such as Biktarvy and its pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) portfolio. The company raised its full-year HIV business growth guidance to 12%, up from its earlier estimate of 9% to 10%. Scotiabank raised its Gilead price target to $200 from $177 and kept an ‘Outperform’ rating, suggesting a 18% upside possibility from the stock’s last close. Truist also increased its target to $181 from $158 while maintaining a ‘Buy’ rating. Retail sentiment around the stock improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’. ExxonMobil Rides On Refining Strength And Higher Dividends ExxonMobil stock also hit a record high of $188.50 after the energy producer reported adjusted Q3 earnings of $4.23 per share, above the $4.03 analyst consensus. Revenue totaled $110.50 billion. ExxonMobil's Energy Products division saw adjusted earnings rise to $9.05 billion, more than doubling from the previous quarter. Higher refining profits and full use of its U.S. Gulf Coast facilities helped drive the growth. Meanwhile, oil production from Guyana's Stabroek Block passed the 1-billion-barrel mark. The company raised its quarterly dividend by 3.8% to $1.07 per share and plans to continue its $20 billion share-repurchase program in 2027. Retail sentiment around the stock shifted to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’. So far this year, MO, GILD and XOM stocks have gained between 35% and 55%. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services.
